children.text: Liliw is a small Laguna hill town that has made slippers since
. Slipper shops line Gat Tayaw Street, and a red-brick Baroque church, Spanish-era houses, and waterfalls on the slopes of Mount Banahaw can all be covered in a single day.
Liliw is a hill town in southeastern Laguna, on the northern slopes of Mount Banahaw. At roughly
above sea level it is a little cooler than Manila, and it lies about
100km
south of the capital. The population is about 40,000 as of the
census, and the town's name is said to come from an old story: when the founder Gat Tayaw planted a pole, a bird landed on it and sang "liw, liw."
What made Liliw famous is its slippers. The industry is said to have begun in

, when Casiano Pisueña made the first pair from coconut husk and tire rubber, and he is still honored as the "Father of Slippers." Shops along Gat Tayaw Street in the town center sell sandals, espadrilles, wedges, and leather shoes, many in colorful designs with woven fabric and flower trim, and Filipinos make a point of coming here to buy from the "slipper capital."
In the middle of town stands the Saint John the Baptist Church, with its striking red-brick facade. It began as a mission settlement in
and a stone church was built in the mid-17th century; it survived the
earthquake and the
fire and was restored, keeping its Baroque look today. In the lanes around the church, wooden-shuttered, balconied Spanish-era houses remain, and some now serve as restaurants and cafés.

It suits travelers who want slipper shopping, Spanish-era architecture, a stroll through a country town, and icy mountain stream water all in one trip. A day trip from Manila is easy, and many people combine it with the Nagcarlan Underground Cemetery next door. Be aware, though, that this is a quiet town, and anyone expecting beaches or large resorts may find it dull.

blocks.title: Slipper shopping on Gat Tayaw Street

children.text: Slipper shops line both sides of the main street through town. The most common rubber and fabric slippers start at
for three pairs, while flower-trimmed sandals and espadrilles run about
. Designs and prices vary from shop to shop, so it's fun to walk the street and compare two or three.

The red-brick facade, a relief of the baptism scene, and the tall bell tower are the town's symbols. Entry is free, and inside are three altars and old saints' statues arranged simply. In the slanting light of morning the brick looks its most beautiful.

A statue of the Virgin stands atop the brick arch that leads into the church forecourt. The spot where the church facade appears through the arch is the best photo location, and the patio has Holy Family sculptures and saints' statues that make for a leisurely walk.

The streets around the church still have Filipino-style old houses with a stone ground floor and a wooden upper story. Looking up at the shutters and ornate railings as you walk, you feel the pace of a small town slow down. Some of the houses now open as restaurants and cafés.
This two-tier waterfall, fed by Mount Banahaw springs, is known for its turquoise pools. From town, take a tricycle to the trailhead, then climb a forest trail for
45 minutes–1 hour
; a guide is required. Access is closed in bad weather.

Beside the road toward Nagcarlan, this resort uses cold mountain spring water and is a good place to cool your feet on a hot day. Entrance fees and opening hours change from time to time, so check before you go.

Flower-shaped cookies made from arrowroot (uraro) starch are known for their melt-in-the-mouth texture, and the coconut spirit lambanog is sold in fruit-flavored versions such as lipote. Along with slippers, they are the most popular souvenirs.
The town's biggest event is held every
late April
around Gat Tayaw Street. It features a storefront decoration contest, a parade, a slipper fashion show, and uraro-cookie-making demonstrations. Lodging and transport are crowded during this period.
Leave Manila (bus to Santa Cruz or San Pablo from PITX, Buendia, or Cubao; by car, take SLEX)
Arrive in Liliw and visit the Saint John the Baptist Church and Milagrosa Arch first
Walk Gat Tayaw Street, comparing two or three slipper shops and shopping
Lunch at a restaurant in a restored old house
Look at old houses in the town's lanes and try uraro cookies as a snack
Buy souvenirs (uraro cookies, lambanog, slippers), then head home
Arrive in Manila (it may take longer on weekends because of return traffic)
To reach Kilangin Falls, you need to leave by tricycle right after lunch, and the round-trip trek adds up to another
3–4 hours
to set aside. If you include the falls, finish the church and shopping in the morning and leave early.

items.title: 2 days, 1 night
items.subtitle: Unhurried, with a waterfall trek and neighboring towns

children.text: Arrive in Liliw, visit the church and shop on Gat Tayaw Street
Lunch at an old-house restaurant, then visit the Nagcarlan Underground Cemetery next door
Check in at lodging in town or San Pablo; dinner at a local restaurant
Start early for the Kilangin Falls trek and a cold-water swim
Buy any remaining souvenirs and leave for Manila
With one night you can visit the falls without rushing, and the long evening lets you enjoy the town's atmosphere at an easy pace.
Take a bus bound for Santa Cruz (Laguna) from PITX, Buendia, or Cubao in Manila. It takes about
2 hours 30 minutes–3 hours 30 minutes
, and the one-way fare is about
In Santa Cruz, transfer to a jeepney marked "Liliw"; the ride takes about
30–45 minutes
and costs about
. Jeepneys run from early morning until around
7 PM
You can also come by way of San Pablo. Take a Lucena-bound bus and get off in front of SM San Pablo, take a tricycle (about
) to the jeepney stop, and then ride a Liliw jeepney for another
45 minutes–1 hour
Fares and routes change often. Check the latest information from the bus company and terminal before you leave. Jeepneys stop running early in the evening, so book your return ride before
5–6 PM
to be safe.
It is about
from Manila and usually takes
2 hours 30 minutes–3 hours 30 minutes

. Take SLEX south, then turn onto the national road toward San Pablo or Santa Cruz. The town roads are narrow and parking near the church is small, so on weekends the roadside in front of shops fills up; arrive early. The mountain road between Nagcarlan and Liliw has many sharp curves.

With three to five or more people, it is easier to charter a van for the day from Manila or Laguna and combine Liliw, the Nagcarlan Underground Cemetery, and the waterfall. Day-charter rates vary a lot with vehicle type and distance, so negotiate in advance.
You can walk around the town center. For farther places such as the Kilangin Falls trailhead or farms on the outskirts, take a tricycle; travelers report about
(up to three people) to Esmeris Farm. Negotiate a half-day charter.
The best time for Liliw is the dry season,
November–May
. In
December–February
the mornings and evenings are cooler than in Manila because of the altitude, which makes walking the slipper street comfortable. In
March–May
the days get hotter, but it is also when the waterfall and spring water are most welcome.
In the
June–October
rainy season, afternoon showers are frequent, and typhoons can affect the area in
August–October
. Kilangin Falls closes in bad weather and the mountain trail turns slippery, so it is safest to skip the falls in the rainy season. If a typhoon is forecast, postpone your trip.
The most special time is
late April
, when the Gat Tayaw Slipper Festival takes place. In
it was held on
April 25–27
, and the schedule shifts slightly each year. The town is crowded during the festival and lodging and transport run short, so check dates and book lodging early.

Lodging in town is limited. Small resorts with pools and farm-style stays are scattered on the outskirts, at roughly
per night. For more choice, stay in hotels in San Pablo or Santa Cruz, about
40 minutes–1 hour
away by car. Most travelers come from Manila for the day.

Liliw is famous for sweet snacks. Flower-shaped cookies made from arrowroot (uraro) starch, suman (rice and coconut milk steamed in banana leaf), and fruit-flavored lambanog such as lipote are the signature souvenirs. Pickled vegetables (atsara) and spiced vinegar are also widely sold. Filipino restaurants and cafés in restored old houses cluster in town. The Italian restaurant Arabela keeps coming up in travel reviews; it is said to be busy at weekend lunch and to close early in the evening, so time your visit accordingly.
Don't buy slippers at the first shop; walk the street once and compare prices and finishing. Many shops give a discount if you buy several pairs.
Try them on before you buy. Hand-woven fabric slippers differ from shop to shop in width and strap tightness, so be sure to check the size.
Photos of the church come out best in the morning, and it is polite to keep quiet during Mass. Avoid shorts and sleeveless tops.
Bring plenty of cash. Small shops, tricycles, and jeepneys often accept cash only.
For the falls, prepare shoes you don't mind getting wet, a change of clothes, and a waterproof bag, and agree on the guide fee before setting out.
Many restaurants and shops close early in the evening, so finish your shopping and meals while there is still daylight.
On a day trip from Manila, allow for jeepney intervals and return traffic and leave no later than
4–5 PM
Check the latest announcements before you go for the festival schedule, whether the falls are open, and the fees at the spring retreat.
The forest trail to Kilangin Falls is slippery in the rain and the water can rise suddenly. Access is closed in bad weather, so check in advance to avoid a wasted trip.
The mountain road linking Nagcarlan and Liliw has many sharp curves. Slow down when driving and avoid driving at night.
In the evening, jeepneys and tricycles become scarce. Don't stay late without securing your ride back.
Pickpockets can operate in markets and on busy streets, so keep your phone and wallet in a bag worn in front.
The church is still a place of worship where Mass is held. Refrain from taking photos and moving around during Mass.
The waterfall water is very cold. If you have a heart or respiratory condition, avoid swimming, and wear a life jacket.
